statement_or_definition:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

statement_or_definition:
Let $T$ be self-adjoint on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ whose inner product is linear in the first variable, use the resolvent convention $R_T(z)=(T-zI)^{-1}$, and let $X\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a specified vector subspace. For $f,h\in X$, the scalar resolvent matrix element is

$$r_{f,h}(z):=\langle R_T(z)f,h\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

Given an open real interval $I$, a point $E_0\in I$, and a disk $D$ centered at $E_0$, a local analytic continuation of these matrix elements through $E_0$ is a specified family of holomorphic functions $\widetilde r_{f,h}:D\to\mathbb C$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, for the stated $f,h\in X$. A **meromorphic continuation** on $D$ is instead a specified family $\widetilde r_{f,h}$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, holomorphic on $D$ except for isolated poles. At every crossing point where no pole occurs it is a regular analytic continuation on a smaller neighborhood. For such a meromorphic continuation, if $z_0\in D$ is nonreal and for some $f,h\in X$ the continued function satisfies

$$\widetilde r_{f,h}(z)=(z-z_0)^{-k}q(z)$$

on a punctured neighborhood of $z_0$, for an integer $k\ge1$ and a holomorphic $q$ with $q(z_0)\ne0$, then $z_0$ is a pole of order $k$ of that continued matrix element. Such a pole is called a resonance matrix-element pole for the specified pair $(T,X)$ and continuation. This definition asserts neither that a continuation exists nor that a pole is an eigenvalue of $T$; the continuation and the chosen test vectors are part of the data.

statement_or_definition:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_0$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex
Hilbert space $H$, with inner product linear in its first variable and
$\inf\sigma(H_0)>-\infty$. Let $g\in H$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and define
$P_g:H\to H$ by $P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g$. Put
$H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda P_g$ on $D(H_\lambda)=D(H_0)$ and
$R_0(z)=(H_0-zI)^{-1}$. Then $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint. For every
$z\in\rho(H_0)$ such that
$d_\lambda(z):=1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle\ne0$, one has
$z\in\rho(H_\lambda)$ and
$$R_\lambda(z):=(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}=R_0(z)-\frac{\lambda R_0(z)P_gR_0(z)}{1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle}.$$
For real $E<\inf\sigma(H_0)$ and $g\ne0$, $E$ is an eigenvalue of $H_\lambda$
if and only if $d_\lambda(E)=0$; in that case the eigenspace is one-dimensional.

statement_or_definition:
If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain (A complex domain is a nonempty connected open subset of $\mathbb C$), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

statement_or_definition:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$. Then every nonreal number belongs to
$\rho(T)$: $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R\subseteq\rho(T)$. More precisely, for
$z=a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $b\ne0$, and every $x\in D(T)$,
$$\|(T-z)x\|^2=\|(T-a)x\|^2+b^2\|x\|^2 ,$$
and consequently $\|R_T(z)\|\le 1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$. In particular
$\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$.
